A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Hydra-NeXt. All 13 pages of each version, including supplementary text, equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison. Existing content can be matched despite reflow and section renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hydra-NeXt results on Bench2Drive and NAVSIM, component ablations, runtime measurements and qualitative driving examples, including supplementary results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds diffusion-scheduler measurements and experiments with a CARLA-Garage-trained variant in Tables 11–12.

M1.justification: The original architecture, losses and nearest-neighbor refinement remain unchanged. Supplementary Sections 9 and 11 add a DDIM inference option and a TF++ adaptation: its longitudinal head is replaced with the trajectory decoder, diffusion outputs are fused with controls, and three models are ensembled. These are bounded procedural extensions.

E1.justification: v2 adds training experiments using CARLA-Garage demonstrations from PDM-Lite, described as smoother than the Think2Drive demonstrations. This extends the represented demonstration distribution within the existing autonomous-driving task; Bench2Drive and NAVSIM coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 12 newly compares the adapted Hydra-NeXt model against TF++ and SimLingo. Neither appeared as an evaluated comparator in v1. Comparator membership in the original Bench2Drive and NAVSIM tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: The added experiments evaluate 20-step DDIM alongside 100-step DDPM and introduce inference with a three-model ensemble for the TF++ adaptation. Existing evaluation metrics and protocols are retained. The new CARLA-Garage section does not fully specify its training and evaluation settings.

E4.justification: Section 9 and Table 11 add a targeted scheduler comparison measuring latency against Driving Score and Success Rate. This extends the existing efficiency analysis. Earlier component, prediction-frequency, proposal-count and individual-policy ablations, together with qualitative examples, are retained.

E5.justification: Table 12 newly specifies that TF++ and the adapted Hydra-NeXt ensemble three models trained with different seeds. This adds seed and model-count information for ensembling, rather than uncertainty estimates from repeated evaluations. Neither version reports confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original results remain unchanged. Table 11 adds the DDIM operating point: 243.9 ms latency, 64.87 DS and 46.63 SR. Table 12 adds the adapted model's 86.00 DS/68.18 SR, TF++'s 84.21/67.27 and SimLingo's 85.94/66.82. These extend the results under added configurations and training data, without establishing a same-setting gain over v1.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the supplementary loss formulations in Equations 1–6 are unchanged. The added scheduler and TF++ implementation discussions introduce no new mathematical definitions, derivations, assumptions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claimed unification of trajectory prediction, control prediction and refinement, together with the same Bench2Drive and NAVSIM performance claims. The supplementary extensions do not redefine the headline contributions.

C2.justification: v1 identifies diffusion latency as a limitation requiring optimization. v2 retains that discussion but adds the interpretation that scheduler choices can make diffusion efficient with a modest performance tradeoff (Section 9). The original limitations paragraph is otherwise unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents the 20-step DDIM configuration with Flash-attention, the TF++ head replacement and control fusion, and the three-model ensemble. These provide implementation information for the added variants. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware disclosures and the promised code-release statement are unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to DDIM and SimLingo and expands its relationship to TF++ through implementation and comparison. The additional bibliography entry for Hidden biases of end-to-end driving models duplicates a work already cited in v1. The main related-work discussion remains substantively stable.

P1.justification: The main text receives limited wording edits, expanded affiliations and an acknowledgement. Two supplementary sections are inserted, renumbering the retained NAVSIM, visualization and limitations sections. There is no extensive rewriting or narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 adds compact Tables 11 and 12 and adjusts nearby text flow, table spacing and captions. All original figures and tables are retained; the architecture diagrams, ablation chart and driving visualizations are unchanged.

improvement.justification: Table 11 provides useful evidence addressing v1's stated diffusion-latency limitation: latency falls from 528.3 to 243.9 ms, with reported DS/SR decreasing from 65.89/48.20 to 64.87/46.63. The additional training-data and baseline comparison broadens applicability evidence, although simultaneous changes to data, architecture and ensembling limit attribution, and its settings are briefly documented. These focused additions improve practical evaluation while leaving the core evidence intact.
